title: Short Stuff: Friends of Dorothy
summary: Short Stuff slang edition on the phrase "friends of Dorothy," a coded term for a gay person. The hosts note the phrase was used for coded communication when being gay was shameful and dangerous. They weigh candidate namesakes: Dorothy King, a early twentieth-century London socialite whose parties attracted gay men; Dorothy Parker, a New York and Los Angeles figure who supported gay people and civil rights; and Dorothy Dean, a Black New York socialite connected to Andy Warhol's circle who worked the door at Max's Kansas City. They conclude any of them could fit at different times. The winner is Dorothy Gale from L. Frank Baum's Wizard of Oz, whose colorful-world transformation and friendships with unconventional men made her a gay icon, and whose story is linked to Judy Garland, a major gay icon. The hosts discuss Garland's funeral, the Stonewall Riots that same night (a contested link), and the phrase's decline. They close with a late-1980s Navy and Army intelligence witch hunt for gay servicemembers, in which investigators, reportedly chasing a real "Dorothy" who helped gay service members, never found her.

segments.title: Opening and meaning of the phrase
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the slang edition and explain that 'friends of Dorothy' means a gay person, and that coded slang was needed because being gay was shameful and dangerous.

segments.title: Dorothy King and Dorothy Parker candidates
segments.summary: Discussion of Dorothy King, an early twentieth-century London socialite who hosted parties for gay men, and Dorothy Parker, who was associated with gay communities in New York and Los Angeles and supported civil rights.

segments.title: Dorothy Dean candidate
segments.summary: Dorothy Dean, a Black New York socialite in Andy Warhol's circle who worked the door at Max's Kansas City, is presented as another possible namesake.

segments.title: Winner: Dorothy Gale from Wizard of Oz
segments.summary: The hosts reveal Dorothy Gale from L. Frank Baum's Wizard of Oz as the winning namesake, citing her transformation from a black and white world to a colorful one and her friendships with unconventional men in the books.

segments.title: Judy Garland as gay icon
segments.summary: Judy Garland, who starred in the film, is described as a major gay icon, with her funeral, a Rufus Wainwright tour, and the contested link between her death and the Stonewall Riots discussed.

segments.title: Decline of slang and military witch hunt
segments.summary: The hosts note the slang has largely faded. They describe a late-1980s Navy and Army intelligence witch hunt for gay servicemembers, led by Vice Admiral Joseph S. Donald, and an account of investigators chasing a supposed Dorothy who never was found.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the episode and sign off with the show's credits.
